AF: Small: RUI: Unifying Self-Assembly Through Tile Automata
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Self-assembly is the bottom-up process by which simple, unorganized components autonomously combine to form larger, more complex structures. This process is abundant in nature, and is a key underlying mechanism for the construction of biological organisms. Researchers are also turning to self-assembly technology for the precise design of ever smaller and more complex nanoscale devices. Thus, self-assembly is emerging as a fundamental tool for nanotechnology.

Of particular interest is algorithmic self-assembly in which local interactions between objects carry out sophisticated computation to efficiently assemble target shapes and patterns. Fully understanding the power and control of self-assembly systems presents the possibility of designing molecular algorithms for precise and efficient manipulation of matter at the nanoscale. A number of experimentally motivated models of algorithmic self-assembly have been proposed with different efficiencies and capabilities. Developing theory towards a better understanding of these models is the focus of this project.

In this proposal the PIs propose a framework for unifying the diverse set of established, experimentally motivated models of algorithmic hierarchical self-assembly. The proposed framework involves the introduction of a mathematically abstracted model of algorithmic self-assembly termed Tile Automata that combines the geometric growth of 2-handed self-assembly, as seen within a number of tile self-assembly models, with local state changes rules, as seen in cellular automata systems such as Conway's Game of Life. This project aims to develop fundamental lemmas and theorems within this model to grow the Tile Automata framework into a powerful tool for proving surprising results within more complex but experimentally motivated models, as well as prove connections between previously distinct models by way of constant-scale simulation results.

In tandem with the theoretical projects depicted in this proposal, a major goal of this project is to increase research participation among students at the University of Texas - Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) and increase the number of UTRGV undergraduate and masters students who enroll in computer science Ph.D. programs. This project details ongoing plans to use student-focused research seminars aimed at introducing and retaining undergraduate student participation and co-authorship. The project further details a number of additional outreach activities aimed at engaging undergraduate researchers, such as the formation of a research-focused hackathon termed Hack-Research, which the PIs plan to deploy here at UTRGV as a part of this project. The PIs have a proven track record of using research seminars to foster student participation in research. Further, the merger of UT-Pan American and UT-Brownsville to form UT-Rio Grande Valley has yielded the largest Hispanic-serving institution in the United States, where both PIs are located. Thus, this project offers a rare opportunity to make a substantial impact on broadening participation among under-represented minority groups in the field of Computer Science.

DNA self-assembly technology is emerging as a powerful tool to manipulate matter at the nanoscale. This tool could be applied to various practical applications such as the mass fabrication of nanoscale devices or molecular computing. Further, self-assembly is a fundamental phenomenon that dictates how complex organisms can grow from simple molecules, implying that further understanding of self-assembly helps in understanding some of nature's greatest mysteries.

The University of Texas - Rio Grande Valley, located in the South Texas Rio Grande Valley area, has more than 30,000 students, with a 90% Hispanic and 55% female student population. UTRGV, is the largest Hispanic-serving institution in the US. A primary goal of this proposal is to increase the research activity of UTRGV Computer Science students by developing a large portion of the orignal research for this proposal within the environment of student-centered research seminars. The PIs also plan to expand participation in research by initiating a new style of research-focussed hack-a-thon at UTRGV. Due to the nature of the UTRGV student body, these plans will help broaden participation in post-graduate Computer Science among under-represented minority groups.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Complexity, Scale, and Benchmarks in Algorithmic Self-Assembly
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Self-assembly is a bottom-up process in which simple, unorganized components autonomously combine to form large, complex structures. This process is found throughout nature as a key underlying mechanism for the construction of biological organisms. Researchers are also turning to self-assembly as a method for the precise design of complex nanoscale devices, making self-assembly an emerging technique in nanotechnology.

Of particular interest is algorithmic self-assembly in which local interactions between objects carry out sophisticated computation to efficiently assemble target shapes and patterns. Fully understanding the power and control of self-assembly systems presents the possibility of designing molecular algorithms for precise and efficient manipulation of matter at the nanoscale. The goal of this project is to develop the mathematics of abstract self-assembly models that are motivated by experimental reality. As these systems are computationally universal, this mathematical study lies in the intersection of mathematics and computer science.

In this proposal the PIs present a research plan to explore the capabilities and complexity of a family of mathematical models of tile-based self-assembly motivated by current technology in DNA nanotechnology. This exploration centers around three types of problems (combinatorial, algorithmic, and complexity-theoretic) that each characterize these models in distinct ways. Preliminary results in these three areas provide new ideas for future efforts, including the resolution of long-standing open problems in the field. We complement this theoretical focus with preliminary wet lab results and proposed future experiments.

In tandem with the theoretical projects depicted in this proposal, a major goal of this project is to increase research participation among students at the University of Texas - Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) and increase the number of UTRGV undergraduate and masters students who enroll in computer science Ph.D. programs. This project details ongoing plans to use student-focused research seminars aimed at introducing and retaining undergraduate student participation and co-authorship. The PIs have a proven track record with utilizing such seminars to foster student participation in research. Further, the merger of UT-Pan American and UT-Brownsville to form UT-Rio Grande Valley has yielded the largest Hispanic-serving institution in the United States, where all three PIs are located. Thus, this project offers a rare opportunity to make a substantial impact on broadening participation among under-represented minority groups in the field of Computer Science.

DNA self-assembly technology is emerging as a powerful tool to manipulate matter at the nanoscale, and has a broad range of practical applications, including the mass fabrication of nanoscale devices and molecular computing. On the other hand, self-assembly is a fundamental phenomenon that dictates how complex organisms can grow from simple molecules, and further understanding of self-assembly helps in understanding some of nature's greatest mysteries.

The University of Texas - Rio Grande Valley, located in the South Texas Rio Grande Valley area, has more than 30,000 students, with a 90% Hispanic and 55% female student population. UTRGV, is the largest Hispanic-serving institution in the US. A primary goal of this proposal is to increase the research activity of UTRGV Computer Science students by developing a large portion of the theory and experimental research for this proposal within the environment of student-centered research seminars. The PIs plan to further develop current research seminars to involve a larger number of students in original research. Due to the nature of the UTRGV student body, this plan will help broaden participation in post-graduate Computer Science among under-represented minority groups.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Complexity, Scale, and Benchmarks in Hierarchical Self-Assembly
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Self-assembly is the bottom-up process by which simple, unorganized components autonomously combine to form larger, more complex structures. This process is abundant in nature, and is a key underlying mechanism for the construction of biological organisms. Researchers are also turning to self-assembly technology for the precise design of complex nanoscale devices [5, 45, 46, 53, 65, 76, 83, 93], making self-assembly an emerging tool for nanotechnology.
Of particular interest is algorithmic self-assembly in which local interactions between objects carry out sophisticated computation to efficiently assemble target shapes and patterns. Fully understanding the power and control of self-assembling systems enables the possibility of precise, efficient, and algorithmic manipulation of matter at the nanoscale. Developing models and theory towards this goal that are closely tied to experimental reality is the focus of this project.
In this proposal, we present a research plan to explore the novel capabilities available to three models of hierarchical tile-based self-assembly motivated by current experimental technology. In hierarchical tile assembly, initial system monomers combine to form larger and more complex polymers that, in turn, act as monomers that combine into even larger polymers. Our preliminary results demonstrate that the novel capabilities of hierarchical models imply techniques and results impossible in traditional non-hierarchical or seeded models of tile assembly. We complement this theoretical focus with preliminary wet lab results and proposed future experiments, as well as software development projects.
In tandem with the theoretical and experimental work proposed, a major goal of this project is to increase research participation among students at the University of Texas - Rio Grande Valley and increase the throughput of undergraduate and masters students who pursue careers in computer science research, including continuing on to Ph.D. programs. This project details ongoing plans to encourage such participation based on student-focused research seminars aimed at introducing and retaining undergraduate student participation and co-authorship. The merger of UT-Pan American and UT-Brownsville to form UT-Rio Grande Valley has yielded the largest Hispanic-serving institution in the United States, where all three PIs are located. Thus, this project offers a rare opportunity to make a substantial impact on broadening participation among under-represented minority groups in the field of Computer Science.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Self-assembly of Shapes at Constant Scale Using Repulsive Forces
INTELLCONT.TITLE_SECONDARY: Unconventional Computation and Natural Computation: 16th International Conference, UCNC 2017, Fayetteville, AR, USA, June 5-9, 2017, Proceedings
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: The algorithmic self-assembly of shapes has been considered in several models of self-assembly. For the problem of shape construction, we consider an extended version of the Two-Handed Tile Assembly Model (2HAM), which contains positive (attractive) and negative (repulsive) interactions. As a result, portions of an assembly can become unstable and detach. In this model, we utilize fuel-efficient computation to perform Turing machine simulations for the construction of the shape. In this paper, we show how an arbitrary shape can be constructed using an asymptotically optimal number of distinct tile types (based on the shape’s Kolmogorov complexity). We achieve this at O(1) scale factor in this straightforward model, whereas all previous results with sublinear scale factors utilize powerful self-assembly models containing features such as staging, tile deletion, chemical reaction networks, and tile activation/deactivation. Furthermore, the computation and construction in our result only creates constant-size garbage assemblies as a byproduct of assembling the shape.
